Q: FastAPI high-load login: how to handle bcrypt/argon2 hashing without blocking and scaling limits? A:

1. CPU bound execution

  • We don't want CPU bound code block the main loop, so if you use FastAPI, use run_in_threadpool which have the same effect when using ThreadPoolExecutor + run_in_executor.
  • The rule of thumb use multiple process for blocking code, but don't overdo it or you will lose performance. Benchmark application such as wrk is your friend.
  • If the code is sufficiently optimized and we still maxed out all cores / vcpu, then we need more machine / vm, no amount of code or "background workers" will solve this.

2. Good practice when handling password

  • Argon2id is the gold standard nowadays.
  • Rate limit login endpoint is a must.
  • Implement MFA or (even better) passwordless option like FIDO2/WebAuthn so we can extend session lifetime while maintaining security. In this context we get less password hashing.
  • Dedicated idP (identity provider) or dedicated auth service is the way to go if your traffic is sufficiently large.

Bonus: sample FastAPI code using run_in_threadpool

from argon2 import PasswordHasher
from fastapi import FastAPI, status
from fastapi.concurrency import run_in_threadpool
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

class HashRequest(BaseModel):
    password: str = Field(..., min_length=1, description="Plain-text password to hash")

class HashResponse(BaseModel):
    hash: str = Field(..., description="Argon2 hash of the password")

app = FastAPI(
    title="Argon2 Password Hasher",
    description="Hash password using Argon2",
    version="0.0.1",
)

_hasher = PasswordHasher()

@app.post("/hash", status_code=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
async def hash_password(body: HashRequest) -> HashResponse:
    hashed: str = await run_in_threadpool(_hasher.hash, body.password)
    return HashResponse(hash=hashed)

Q: ESP8266 Deep Sleep wakes up but code doesn’t run after reset A:

This is a well-known and frustrating issue with many ESP8266 modules, especially cheaper NodeMCU clones. Your debug output is the classic signature — rst cause:2, boot mode:(3,6) appears (proving the wake-up reset fires), but the bootloader never hands off to your code. Here's what's likely going on and what to try:

The reset pulse from GPIO16 is too short
This is the most common root cause. When the deep sleep timer expires, GPIO16 pulls RST low, but on some modules the pulse is so brief that the chip partially resets without fully reinitializing its internal registers. The bootloader starts (you see the ets Jan 8 2013 message) but never loads your firmware from flash.

Fix: Add a 100 nF (0.1 µF) ceramic capacitor between RST and GND. This stretches the reset pulse long enough for a clean boot. This is actually recommended in Espressif's hardware design guidelines but many clone boards omit it.

Keep your resistor between D0 and RST as well (470 Ω – 1 kΩ works). The combination of resistor + cap is the most reliable setup.

Also make sure you have a 10 kΩ pull-up from RST to 3.3V if your board doesn't already have one on-board (most NodeMCU boards do, but some clones don't).

The CH340 USB-serial chip may be interfering with RST
On some CH340-based NodeMCU clones, the auto-reset circuit (DTR/RTS through a capacitor to RST) can fight with the GPIO16 wake-up signal. When your serial monitor opens a connection, DTR can hold RST in an ambiguous state.

Test this: Disconnect USB entirely and power the board from an external 3.3V supply (or a USB power bank with no data lines). If deep sleep wake up suddenly works, the CH340 reset circuit is your problem.

Fix options:

  • Cut the trace between the CH340's DTR and the RST capacitor (if you can identify it)

  • Just use external power when running in deep sleep mode

  • Try closing the Serial Monitor before the wake-up cycle

Bad flash chip (clone/counterfeit module issue)
This has been tracked extensively in esp8266/Arduino issue #6007. A developer reported that the same PCB and code worked on 100+ boards from one batch, then completely failed on a new batch. Testing across multiple suppliers showed that out of 8 ESP8266 modules, only 2 woke correctly from deep sleep and the behavior was consistent per-module, not random.

The working theory is that some flash chips on clone modules have slower startup times, so when the ESP tries to read firmware from flash after a deep sleep reset, the flash isn't ready yet and the boot hangs.

Diagnosis: Run this to check your flash chip ID:

Serial.println(ESP.getFlashChipId(), HEX);

If the ID doesn't match a known manufacturer (e.g., Winbond EF, GigaDevice C8), you may have a counterfeit flash chip.

Fix: Try a different board. If you have multiple NodeMCUs, test them all — you may find some work and some don't. Boards from reputable sources (Wemos D1 Mini from the official store, Adafruit Feather HUZZAH, etc.) generally don't have this problem.

Flash mode setting mismatch
Make sure your Arduino IDE board settings match your actual hardware:

  • Flash Mode: Try DOUT instead of QIO. DOUT is slower but more compatible, especially with clone flash chips.

  • Flash Size: Should match your chip (usually 4MB for NodeMCU)

  • Reset Method: Try both "ck" and "nodemcu"

Go to Tools → Flash Mode → DOUT, re-upload, and test again.

Summary / what I'd try in order:

  1. Add 100 nF cap between RST and GND (solves ~60% of cases)

  2. Change Flash Mode to DOUT and re-upload

  3. Test with USB disconnected (external power only)

  4. If none of the above work → try a different board, preferably a name-brand one

This issue has been reported across many forums and GitHub issues going back years, and unfortunately the root cause often comes down to hardware quality. The capacitor fix is the most universally successful software/hardware workaround.
